newsitem.title: UK: Conservative agrees to principles of UK poll debate.
newsitem.headline: Conservative agrees to principles of UK poll debate.

text.p: Britain's Conservatives, facing an uphill battle in the May 1 election, said on Sunday they have agreed to the basic principles of a U.S. style debate between Prime Minister John Major and Labour leader Tony Blair.

But the parties are still disputing whether or not Paddy Ashdown, head of the minority Liberal Democrats should be included, and whether the debate should be held in front of a participating audience.
"So far as we are concerned there is no reason for the debate now not to go ahead," Conservative Party chairman Brian Mawhinney said in a statement.

He added that his party, which wants to limit the debate to Major and Blair, was considering the proposals from two television networks and denied Labour accusations that the Conservatives were posing problems.

"It's very arrogant and very petty of Mr Major to try to exclude Paddy Ashdown. So if we are going to have a debate let's have one that is legal. Let's have one in which the public can participate," Peter Mandelson, Labour's campaign manager told BBC telelvision.

As the major parties squabbled over the debate and traded accusations of sleaze, a new Gallp poll published in The Sunday Telegraph newspaper and the first since Major announced the election last Monday, showed Labour's lead remained at 25.5 points -- enough to give Labour a landslide majority ofter 18 years out of power.
"Labour has the clear backing of a clear majority of voters -- 54.5 percent -- while the Conservatives trail on 29 points. The Liberal Democrats are on 10.5 points," the newspaper said.
"It represents a swing of 16.5 points to Labour since the last election and would give Tony Blair an overall majority of around 250 seats," it added.
The Labour leader, bidding to become the country's youngest prime minister this century, only needs a 4.3 percent swing from the 1992 election for an overall parliamentary majority.
The growing bitterness between the two main parties was plain in Sunday morning television interviews with top figures from both the Conservative and Labour campaign team.

Mandelson renewed the attack on sleaze challenging Major to recall parliament to hear a report by a parliamentary ethics watchdog into the allegations of influence peddling by 10 Conservative members of parliament.

Major's decision to announce the election last week and close parliament on Monday means a report into the allegations cannnot be published before the election unless the government, in an extraordinary climb-down, recalls the House of Commons.
"If he refuses to recall parliament, then that must carry the implication that he's trying to cover up the truth," Mandelson told a BBC interviewer.
But Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine accused Labour on the same programme of trying to stir up the sleaze scandal to distract attention from excellent economic statistics.
